text.p: The peseta, usually well supported by any dollar rise, is shrugging off the U.S. currency's recent strength which analysts see as a clear sign that the future European Monetary Union is already at work.
The dollar's recent appreciation brought the dollar well above 1.70 marks to set a 34-month high.

But the peseta, used to taking advantage of the mark's weakness, remained glued to a tight level between 84.54 and 84.76 per mark, despite the Bank of Spain's suspected intervention on its behalf a week ago.

"Current dollar strength is more against Europe than against Germany, this is why we don't have the intra-European effect of a high-dollar we used to have in the past," said Henrik Lumholdt, chief economist at Bank of America in Madrid.
A more aligned trend in Europe's economies is ensuring that currencies such as the Italian lira and the Spanish peseta cannot gain over the German mark.
"The dollar's strength, which used to support peripherals in the past, doesn't any more," said Valentin Fernandez at Credit Lyonnais in Madrid.
"People buy dollars because they fear a weak euro, and the more likely it is Spain and Italy will enter EMU, the more likely it is we'll have a stronger dollar," he added.
The U.S. dollar was trading on Tuesday around 144 pesetas which compares with levels around 125 at the end of November.
Behind the dollar's bullishness is market expectations of a possible increase in U.S. official rates while they expect German rates to be steady, or -- if anything -- to fall.
The forthcoming Euro, the European single currency, is something markets are already factoring into decisions.
"We have the single currency already in people's minds..what they perceive is a hidden euro," said Lumholdt.

Economists added that further proof of the peseta's new Euro ties was evident in sterling's behaviour. It has been strong, and following the dollar higher as in the past, because the U.K. is not expected to take part in the common currency.
Sterling/mark jumped from 2.5625 per mark on December 5 to trade around 2.7346/56 per mark on Tuesday.
European governments, with growth in their economies depressed by the tight public spending policies required by the Maastricht Treaty, had been in favour of dollar strength to spur growth.

"European countries agreed on the need for the dollar to rise in order to spur growth...Let's say they are happy with the latest five or six month trend. The problem now is they will like it to stop there," said Jose Luis Alzola, economist at Salomon Brothers in London.

In Madrid, exporters have been registering a jump in shares, dealers said. Spanish steel producer Acerinox, for example, outperformed the general index, trading on Tuesday at around 21,290 pesetas from 16,600 on January 27.
The risk now for the Spanish economy, economists agreed, is from inflation spurred by those imported goods denominated in U.S. dollars.
